---
title: "A straight-line mean"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The [conditional-mean page](regression-models.qmd) left $m(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ unrestricted. **Simple linear regression** imposes the straight-line restriction stated below.

In this application, $Y$ is the [Provo word position mean](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data) of log first fixation durations among readers with a retained positive fixation. The predictor is **modeled cloze surprisal**, the negative base-two logarithm of the fitted cloze probability defined in that same discussion. The line consequently describes passage grouped position summaries rather than raw reader trials or the probability of skipping a word.

The response distribution below assumes [independent](../foundations/independence.qmd) rows only when that condition is explicitly stated. Its [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) describes response spread around the line, whereas a coefficient [standard error](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd) describes repeated-sample variation of an estimator.

The key separation is between a straight conditional mean and a Gaussian response distribution around that mean. The Provo fit makes both restrictions visible before its slope is interpreted over the observed surprisal range.

$$
m(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x.
$$

The word *simple* means that the model has one predictor. The word *linear* means that the coefficients enter as a weighted sum.

## Mean function versus response distribution

This equation restricts a conditional mean. It does not yet say how individual position summaries vary around that mean. For instance, both

$$
Y_i\mid X_i=x_i\sim\mathcal N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)
$$

and a Student-$t$ response centered at $\beta_0+\beta_1x_i$ share the same line but make different tail assumptions. The next fitting page uses squared loss, and conventional finite-sample inference later adds independent errors, constant variance, and a normal response. Keeping these pieces separate prevents a plotted line from silently importing a complete probability model.

## Fitting the Provo regression line

We return to the Provo position summaries and center modeled cloze surprisal at its observed mean. Centering makes the intercept correspond to an observed reference point; the [next page](centering-predictors.qmd) derives that equivalence.

```{r}
#| label: fit-provo-simple-regression
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
surprisal_center <- mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - surprisal_center

fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)
coefficient_table <- coef(summary(fit))

stopifnot(
  nrow(provo) == 1593L,
  length(unique(provo$Text_ID)) == 55L,
  isTRUE(all.equal(mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_c), 0, tolerance = 1e-12))
)

coefficient_table
```

The fitted conditional mean is

$$
\widehat m(x_i)
=
\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1(x_i-\overline x).
$$

At mean modeled cloze surprisal, the fitted mean log first fixation duration is `r sprintf("%.4f", coef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]])`. Each additional bit of modeled cloze surprisal is associated with a change of `r sprintf("%.4f", coef(fit)[["cloze_surprisal_c"]])` log milliseconds in the fitted position mean.

The slope is a contrast between conditional means:

$$
m(x+1)-m(x)
=
\{\beta_0+\beta_1(x+1)\}
-\{\beta_0+\beta_1x\}
=\beta_1.
$$

Thus the intercept locates the line, while the slope gives its change per predictor unit.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-simple-regression
#| fig-cap: "Reader-aggregated Provo positions and the fitted straight-line conditional mean."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - surprisal_center
grid$fitted <- predict(fit, newdata = grid)

point_opacity <- 0.22
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.9) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, fitted),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The line summarizes an average item-position association. A potential worry is that the plotted cloud contains nested passages. That concern is well founded: ordinary standard errors do not represent passage clustering, and reader clustering cannot be recovered from this table. We address the remaining passage identifier on the [uncertainty page](linear-regression-uncertainty.qmd).

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which conditional means are compared by the slope?
2. Why does a one-bit increase have the same fitted change everywhere on the line?
3. Does the positive slope show that surprisal causes longer fixations?
4. Which dependence structure remains visible in the table?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The slope compares $m(x+1)$ with $m(x)$: fitted mean log FFD at predictor values one bit apart. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The straight-line restriction makes $m(x+1)-m(x)=\beta_1$ for every $x$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. No. The slope is an observational item-position association and does not identify a causal effect of surprisal. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Passage membership remains visible through `Text_ID`; reader dependence cannot be recovered after aggregation. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [next page](centering-predictors.qmd) changes the reference point without changing the fitted relation.
